title: The contract for sale
subtitle: The Standard Conditions of Sale, deducing title, and what happens when a party defaults
objectives: Explain the core structure of the Standard Conditions of Sale, including formation, deposit, title, and completion
Apply the deposit and completion default rules, including the treatment of interest and the court's discretion over forfeiture
Identify a buyer's available remedies where the seller cannot deduce satisfactory title

leadingAuthorities.role: Gives the court discretion to order the return of a forfeited deposit

leadingAuthorities.citation: Tennaro Ltd v Majorarch Ltd [2003] EWHC 2601 (Ch)
leadingAuthorities.role: Illustrates how the s 49(2) discretion is exercised, and its limits

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Most students can recite '10% deposit, exchange then complete'. What actually gets tested is what happens off that script — a buyer who cannot raise the conventional 10%, a seller who cannot show good title by the contractual date, or a party who simply fails to complete on time. That is where the Standard Conditions of Sale do their real work.

profileHooks.weakApplication: You know the structure. This lesson is weighted towards default scenarios — late completion, a defective title, a deposit dispute — because that is where the exam actually tests understanding.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and be exact about what happens at exchange versus completion, and what the deposit actually is (part payment held as security), before moving on to the default provisions.

overview.hook: Exchange of contracts is often described as the moment a sale becomes 'binding', as though everything after that is administrative. It isn't. The contract that gets exchanged is a detailed set of rules — about deposits, about who bears the risk of a defect in title, about what happens if either side simply fails to turn up on completion day — and a solicitor who treats it as a formality is the one whose client ends up in a dispute.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 24 September 2026 by reference to the Standard Conditions of Sale (5th edition) as commonly incorporated into residential and commercial contracts, and to the Law of Property Act 1925 as amended. Parties may and often do vary these conditions by special condition; this lesson covers the unamended default position.

parts.heading: Formation and the deposit: what actually happens at exchange
parts.voice: practical — walks through the mechanics as a solicitor would explain them to a client
body: A contract for the sale of land does not exist merely because seller and buyer have agreed a price. Under s 2 of the Law of Property (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1989, a contract for the sale of land must be in writing, incorporate all agreed terms in one document (or by reference to another), and be signed by or on behalf of both parties. In practice, conveyancers achieve this by preparing identical contracts, each signed by one party, which are then formally exchanged — that exchange, not the earlier agreement of price, is the moment the contract becomes binding.

The Standard Conditions of Sale (SCS), now in their fifth edition, are the standard-form terms almost universally incorporated by reference into residential (and much commercial) conveyancing, so that the parties do not have to draft every term from scratch. They govern matters including the deposit, the state and condition of the property, the deducing and investigation of title, and the mechanics and consequences of completion.

On exchange, the buyer conventionally pays a deposit of 10% of the purchase price, held by the seller's solicitor as agent for the seller (or, under an amended condition, as stakeholder) until completion. The deposit performs two functions: it is part payment of the price, and it operates as a form of security for the seller if the buyer later fails to complete — which is why, as this lesson covers below, forfeiting it is the seller's standard remedy for a defaulting buyer.

components.definition: The formal process, usually conducted by telephone or in person between solicitors following a fixed protocol, by which two signed copies of an identical contract are exchanged — the moment from which the contract for sale becomes legally binding on both parties.

interaction.prompt: A buyer and seller agree a price over the phone and shake hands, but contracts have not yet been exchanged. Is there a binding contract for the sale of land at this point?
options: No — a binding contract requires a written document, incorporating all terms, signed by both parties and exchanged
Yes — an oral agreement on price is sufficient to bind both parties to a land sale
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. Section 2 LP(MP)A 1989 requires a signed written contract incorporating all the terms; exchange, not a handshake on price, is what creates the binding obligation.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: An oral agreement on price is not enough for land — s 2 LP(MP)A 1989 requires the contract to be in writing, incorporate all terms, and be signed and exchanged before it binds either party.

parts.heading: Title and vacant possession under the Standard Conditions
parts.voice: structural — a reference-style part students will return to
body: Two obligations sit at the centre of the seller's side of the bargain: an obligation to deduce a good title to the property, and (unless the contract says otherwise) an obligation to give vacant possession on completion — that is, to hand the property over free of any occupiers, chattels or rights of occupation not disclosed and accepted by the buyer.

The process by which the seller proves title is called deducing title: the seller (or their solicitor) supplies evidence of ownership — official copies and any relevant documents for registered land, or an epitome of title for unregistered land — for the buyer's solicitor to examine. Where anything in that evidence is unclear, missing or appears defective, the buyer's solicitor raises requisitions on title: formal written queries the seller must answer, or resolve, before completion can safely proceed.

The Standard Conditions set out timetables for each of these steps by reference to the contract date, so that a party who is slow to deduce title or to answer requisitions is themselves in breach of a contractual timetable, not merely being unhelpful. This is a frequently tested distinction: 'deducing title' is the seller's evidential obligation; 'requisitions' are the buyer's mechanism for querying that evidence; and both operate against contractually fixed deadlines, not an open-ended 'as soon as convenient'.

components.label: Title and possession — the core seller obligations
points: Deduce title — supply evidence of ownership (official copies or epitome) within the timetable set by the contract
Respond to requisitions — answer the buyer's formal queries on that evidence, or resolve any defect identified
Give vacant possession on completion — unless the contract expressly provides otherwise
A defect not resolved before completion may entitle the buyer to refuse to complete or to claim a remedy for unsatisfactory title

interaction.prompt: Put these steps in the order they occur under the Standard Conditions' title machinery.
items: Seller deduces title by supplying official copies or an epitome within the contractual timetable
Buyer's solicitor examines the evidence supplied
Buyer's solicitor raises requisitions on any unclear or apparently defective point
Seller answers or resolves the requisitions before completion
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Title has to be deduced before it can be examined, examined before requisitions can sensibly be raised, and requisitions raised before the seller can be expected to answer them.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the order again — examination logically follows deduction of title, and requisitions can only be raised once the buyer's solicitor has actually reviewed what was supplied.

parts.heading: Completion, and interest on late completion
parts.voice: case-narrative — tells the story of a delayed completion before naming the doctrine
body: Completion is the moment legal title actually passes and the balance of the purchase price is paid — typically the working day agreed in the contract, though the Standard Conditions also fix a default completion time (1.00 pm) where the contract itself does not otherwise specify a time.

Consider a straightforward delay: the buyer's mortgage funds are simply not received by the buyer's solicitor in time, and completion, contractually fixed for 2.00 pm, does not happen until the following morning. Neither party disputes the underlying sale will go ahead — the only question is what the delay costs.

The Standard Conditions answer this directly: where completion is delayed by the fault of one party (commonly the buyer, through late funds), the defaulting party must pay the other compensation calculated as interest on the balance of the purchase price outstanding, running from the contractual completion date until actual completion, at the contract rate specified in the conditions (a rate set by reference to a base rate plus a margin). This is not a penalty in the punitive sense — it compensates the non-defaulting party for being kept out of their money.

components.definition: The date (and, absent contrary agreement, the default time of 1.00 pm under the Standard Conditions) fixed in the contract by which completion must take place; a delay past this date by one party's fault triggers the interest compensation mechanism, and may in more serious cases trigger the notice-to-complete machinery.

interaction.prompt: Completion is contractually fixed for 2.00 pm on a Friday. The buyer's mortgage funds arrive late and completion does not occur until 10.00 am the following Monday, through no fault of the seller. What is the seller's standard remedy under the Standard Conditions for this delay?
options: The seller may immediately rescind the contract and keep the property
The seller is entitled to compensation calculated as interest on the outstanding balance for the period of the buyer's delay
The seller has no remedy since the sale did eventually complete
The seller may automatically forfeit the full deposit regardless of the length of delay
interaction.explanation: A short delay caused by one party's fault triggers the interest compensation mechanism under the Standard Conditions, calculated on the outstanding balance for the period of delay — it does not, on its own, entitle the innocent party to rescind or forfeit the deposit outright.

parts.heading: Forfeiture of the deposit and the court's discretion
parts.voice: Socratic — poses the harder default scenario before resolving it
body: Now push the same facts further: instead of a short delay, the buyer simply cannot complete at all, perhaps because a mortgage offer has fallen through entirely and no alternative funding can be found. What happens to the 10% deposit already paid?

The general position under the Standard Conditions is that a seller faced with a buyer's failure to complete may forfeit the deposit and resell the property, in addition to pursuing the buyer for any further loss on resale. This reflects the deposit's security function described in Part 1 — it exists precisely to protect the seller against exactly this risk.

But forfeiture is not automatic or beyond challenge. Section 49(2) of the Law of Property Act 1925 gives the court a discretion to order repayment of a deposit (or part of it) to the buyer, notwithstanding that it would otherwise be forfeit, where the court considers it just to do so. This discretion is exercised sparingly — courts are conscious that a wide power to unwind forfeiture would undermine the deposit's whole purpose as security — and is more likely to be exercised where the deposit paid was unconventionally large, or where the buyer's default was minor relative to the sum at stake.

Tennaro Ltd v Majorarch Ltd illustrates how narrow this discretion actually is in practice: the court confirmed that s 49(2) is not a general fairness override to be invoked whenever forfeiture feels harsh, and that a conventional 10% deposit forfeited following a straightforward failure to complete will not typically be disturbed.

components.text: Where the court refuses to grant specific performance of a contract, or in any action for the return of a deposit, the court may, if it thinks fit, order the repayment of any deposit.
elements: A contract for the sale of land has been made
A deposit has been paid and would otherwise be forfeit
The court considers, in its discretion, that it is just to order its return, in whole or in part

components.factsShort: A buyer paid a deposit and failed to complete; the seller forfeited the deposit and the buyer sought its return under s 49(2), arguing forfeiture was unfair in the circumstances.
components.ratioShort: The s 49(2) discretion is exercised narrowly and is not a general fairness override; a conventional deposit forfeited after a straightforward default is unlikely to be ordered returned.

expanded.facts: The buyer paid a conventional deposit on exchange but was unable to complete the purchase. The seller forfeited the deposit in accordance with the contract terms. The buyer sought repayment under s 49(2), arguing more generally that retaining the full deposit was disproportionate to the seller's actual loss.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The court confirmed that the s 49(2) discretion exists to prevent injustice in genuinely exceptional circumstances, not to reopen the ordinary consequences of a straightforward default on a conventional deposit. The deposit's function as agreed security for performance would be undermined if courts routinely relieved defaulting buyers of its consequences.
expanded.significance: Tennaro is regularly cited for the proposition that s 49(2) is a narrow safety valve rather than a broad fairness jurisdiction — a point that distinguishes a strong exam answer (which explains why the discretion will not normally help a defaulting buyer) from a weak one (which simply asserts 'the court has discretion' without engaging with how narrowly it is used).

interaction.prompt: In the passage below adapted from the reasoning in Tennaro, highlight the sentence that states the ratio.
interaction.passage: The buyer argues that retaining the deposit is disproportionate. The discretion under section 49(2) exists to prevent injustice in genuinely exceptional circumstances, not to reopen the ordinary consequences of a straightforward default on a conventional deposit. The buyer's application for repayment is refused.
interaction.ratioSentence: The discretion under section 49(2) exists to prevent injustice in genuinely exceptional circumstances, not to reopen the ordinary consequences of a straightforward default on a conventional deposit.

parts.heading: When the seller cannot deduce satisfactory title
parts.voice: direct — sets up the buyer-side trap the tests will probe
body: So far the default scenarios have assumed the buyer is the one who fails. The Standard Conditions also address the reverse case: what happens if it is the seller who cannot make good on the contract, because title turns out to be defective — an undisclosed restrictive covenant surfaces, or a requisition reveals a genuine gap in the chain of ownership that cannot be resolved before completion.

Where the seller cannot show title in accordance with the contract, and the defect is not one the buyer agreed to accept, the buyer is not left simply to complete regardless and hope for the best. Depending on the seriousness of the defect and the contract's terms, the buyer's options typically include: rescinding the contract and recovering the deposit with interest, seeking specific performance with an abatement of the price to reflect the defect, or claiming damages for breach where the seller has failed to fulfil the obligation to deduce good title.

The trap in exam fact patterns is assuming that any imperfection in title is fatal, or conversely that a buyer must simply accept whatever title is offered once exchange has happened. Neither is right: the Standard Conditions draw a real distinction between defects that were disclosed (or ought reasonably to have been discovered before exchange, and so are treated as accepted) and defects that only emerge afterwards and materially affect the value or enjoyment of the property — it is the latter category that opens up the buyer's remedies described above.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often assume that once contracts are exchanged, a buyer has no choice but to complete regardless of any title defect discovered afterwards, because 'the contract is binding'.
components.whyItsWrong: A binding contract is not the same as an unconditional obligation to accept any title however defective. The seller's obligation to deduce good title is itself a contractual term; a serious, undisclosed defect in title is a breach of that term, and the Standard Conditions and general contract law give the buyer real remedies — rescission, specific performance with abatement, or damages — rather than forcing completion on defective terms.

interaction.prompt: After exchange, a buyer's solicitor discovers an undisclosed restrictive covenant materially affecting the buyer's intended use of the property, which the seller cannot resolve before the completion date. What is the most accurate statement of the buyer's position?
options: The buyer must complete regardless, since the contract became binding on exchange
The buyer has no remedy because requisitions were not raised before exchange
The buyer may have remedies such as rescission, specific performance with abatement of price, or damages, because the seller's obligation to deduce good title has arguably been breached
The buyer's only option is to renegotiate the price informally with no legal basis to insist on it
interaction.trapExplanation: The tempting wrong answer treats exchange as if it settles everything, including title quality. It does not — the seller's obligation to deduce good title survives exchange, and a genuine undisclosed defect discovered afterwards is a breach opening up the buyer's standard remedies.
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. A material, undisclosed title defect surfacing after exchange is a breach of the seller's obligation to deduce good title, giving the buyer real remedies rather than an unqualified duty to complete.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Exchange does not force the buyer to accept any title, however defective. Think about what obligation the seller has actually failed to meet, and what that breach typically opens up for the buyer.

testPool.prompt: Under s 2 of the Law of Property (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1989, what is required for a contract for the sale of land to be validly formed?
options: An oral agreement on the price, confirmed by conduct
A written document, incorporating all agreed terms, signed by or on behalf of both parties
A signed document from the seller alone, with the buyer's assent implied by payment of a deposit
Registration of the agreement at HM Land Registry
testPool.explanation: Section 2 requires the contract to be in writing, to incorporate all the terms the parties have expressly agreed in one document (or by reference), and to be signed by or on behalf of each party.

testPool.prompt: What is the conventional level of deposit paid by a buyer on exchange of contracts under the Standard Conditions of Sale?
options: 5% of the purchase price
10% of the purchase price
25% of the purchase price
A fixed sum of £1,000 regardless of price
testPool.explanation: 10% is the conventional deposit figure under the Standard Conditions, functioning both as part payment of the price and as security for the seller against the buyer's default.

testPool.prompt: What best describes the function of the deposit paid on exchange of contracts?
options: It is purely a fee for the seller's solicitor's time in preparing the contract
It serves both as part payment of the purchase price and as security for the seller if the buyer later fails to complete
It is refundable in full to the buyer regardless of the reason completion fails to occur
It only becomes payable once completion has actually taken place
testPool.trapExplanation: Students sometimes treat the deposit as a simple advance payment with no further significance. Its dual function — part payment and security — is exactly why forfeiture is available to a seller facing a defaulting buyer.
testPool.explanation: Recognising the deposit's security function is what makes sense of the forfeiture rules covered later in this lesson.

testPool.prompt: A seller's solicitor supplies official copies of the title within the timetable set by the contract. The buyer's solicitor reviews them and spots an apparently unresolved restriction on the proprietorship register. What is the correct next step?
options: Proceed straight to completion, since official copies were supplied on time
Raise a requisition on title querying the restriction before completion
Rescind the contract immediately without further enquiry
Report the matter directly to HM Land Registry rather than the seller
testPool.explanation: An unresolved point on the title evidence supplied is precisely what requisitions are for — a formal query to the seller, raised within the contractual timetable, before completion proceeds.

testPool.prompt: What does the Standard Conditions' default completion time of 1.00 pm actually determine?
options: The time by which contracts must be exchanged
The time by which completion must occur where the contract itself does not specify a different time
The time by which the deposit must be paid
The statutory deadline for registering the transfer at HM Land Registry
testPool.explanation: Absent a different time agreed in the contract, the Standard Conditions fix 1.00 pm as the default time by which completion must take place on the agreed completion date.

testPool.prompt: Completion is contractually fixed for 1.00 pm on a Tuesday. Through the buyer's fault, completion actually occurs at 9.00 am the following Wednesday. Neither party wishes to end the transaction. What compensation mechanism applies under the Standard Conditions?
options: The buyer must pay the seller interest on the outstanding balance for the period of delay
The seller must return the deposit in full as a penalty for delay
No compensation is payable provided completion eventually occurs
The buyer forfeits the property entirely and the sale is treated as void
testPool.explanation: A delay caused by one party's fault triggers the interest compensation mechanism on the outstanding balance for the period of delay — a straightforward, short default does not on its own entitle the seller to treat the contract as at an end.

testPool.prompt: Why is interest payable on late completion under the Standard Conditions best understood as compensatory rather than punitive?
options: Because it is calculated purely at the discretion of the seller's solicitor with no fixed method
Because it reflects the cost of the non-defaulting party being kept out of money they were contractually due, calculated by reference to a specified rate on the outstanding balance
Because it is only payable if the defaulting party acted dishonestly
Because it replaces the deposit entirely once a delay occurs
testPool.trapExplanation: Framing the interest provision as a punishment for wrongdoing is a common misreading. It is calculated mechanically on the outstanding balance for the period of delay, reflecting the time value of money withheld, not the defaulting party's state of mind.
testPool.explanation: The compensatory character of the interest provision distinguishes it from forfeiture of the deposit, which is triggered by a more serious failure to complete at all.

testPool.prompt: A buyer's mortgage offer is withdrawn shortly before completion and no alternative funding can be arranged; the buyer cannot complete at all. What is the seller's standard remedy under the Standard Conditions?
options: The seller may forfeit the deposit and resell the property, pursuing the buyer for any further loss on resale
The seller's only remedy is to sue for specific performance
The seller must return the deposit in full since the buyer's default was not intentional
The seller has no remedy unless the buyer acted fraudulently
testPool.explanation: A genuine failure to complete at all, as opposed to a short delay, engages the deposit's security function directly — the seller may forfeit it and pursue any shortfall on resale as further loss.

testPool.prompt: Which statutory provision gives the court a discretion to order the return of a forfeited deposit?
options: Law of Property Act 1925, s 49(2)
Land Registration Act 2002, s 4
Misrepresentation Act 1967, s 2
Law of Property (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1989, s 2
testPool.explanation: Section 49(2) LPA 1925 is the specific statutory discretion allowing a court to order repayment of a deposit that would otherwise be forfeit, exercised only where the court considers it just to do so.

testPool.prompt: Following Tennaro Ltd v Majorarch Ltd, a buyer who paid a conventional 10% deposit and then simply failed to complete applies under s 49(2) for its return, arguing forfeiture feels harsh. How is this application likely to be treated?
options: Granted automatically, since s 49(2) exists to prevent any unfairness to a defaulting buyer
Likely refused, since the s 49(2) discretion is exercised narrowly and does not disturb the ordinary consequences of a straightforward default on a conventional deposit
Granted, but only if the seller consents
Refused only if the buyer acted in bad faith, and otherwise granted as of right
testPool.trapExplanation: The trap is assuming s 49(2) operates as a general fairness override available whenever forfeiture feels harsh to the defaulting party. Tennaro confirms the opposite — the discretion is a narrow safety valve for genuinely exceptional circumstances, not a routine escape route from a conventional default.
testPool.explanation: A straightforward default on a conventional deposit, without more, is exactly the scenario Tennaro holds the s 49(2) discretion is unlikely to disturb.

testPool.prompt: A buyer paid an unusually large deposit of 30% of the price at the seller's insistence, then suffered a comparatively minor delay in completion due to a short administrative hold-up at their bank. Which factor makes a s 49(2) application for partial return of the deposit comparatively more arguable than in a routine 10% deposit case?
options: The unconventional size of the deposit relative to the modest nature of the default
The fact that a delay occurred at all, regardless of size or deposit amount
The buyer's genuine belief that the delay was minor
The identity of the buyer's mortgage lender
testPool.explanation: Courts are more willing to consider exercising the s 49(2) discretion where the deposit is unconventionally large relative to the seriousness of the default — the disproportion is what can make forfeiture look genuinely unjust, unlike a routine 10% deposit forfeited after a real failure to complete.

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is NOT typically an obligation the seller owes under the Standard Conditions of Sale?
options: To deduce title within the contractual timetable
To give vacant possession on completion, unless the contract provides otherwise
To respond to requisitions raised by the buyer's solicitor
To guarantee the property will increase in value before completion
testPool.trapExplanation: This option is designed to test whether students can distinguish genuine contractual obligations (title, possession, responding to requisitions) from an invented obligation with no basis in the Standard Conditions or general conveyancing law.
testPool.explanation: The seller's obligations concern the legal quality and delivery of the property, not its market performance — there is no such thing as a warranty against a fall in value.

testPool.prompt: After exchange, the buyer's solicitor discovers the seller cannot resolve a genuine, undisclosed defect in title that materially affects the buyer's intended use of the land. Which of the following is a remedy potentially available to the buyer?
options: Rescission of the contract with recovery of the deposit and interest
Automatic forfeiture of the seller's legal costs with no other remedy available
No remedy, since exchange is final regardless of title defects
A claim against the buyer's own solicitor only, with no recourse against the seller
testPool.explanation: A material, unresolved defect in title amounting to a breach of the seller's obligation to deduce good title can open up rescission (with return of the deposit and interest), specific performance with abatement, or damages — not an unqualified duty on the buyer to complete regardless.

testPool.prompt: Under s 49(2) LPA 1925, in what type of proceeding may the court exercise its discretion to order repayment of a deposit?
options: Only in criminal proceedings related to fraud
Where the court refuses specific performance, or in an action for the return of a deposit
Only where both parties jointly apply to the court
Only in proceedings brought by the seller against the buyer's mortgage lender
testPool.explanation: Section 49(2) is engaged specifically where the court refuses to order specific performance, or in an action brought for the return of a deposit — the discretion is not a freestanding remedy available in any type of dispute.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The recurring trap in this lesson is treating exchange of contracts as the point at which every risk is settled. It is not — the deposit, completion timetable, and title obligations all continue to generate real consequences (interest, forfeiture, rescission) depending on exactly how and why a party defaults.
